body.title: One tool registry for git, gh, Jira
body.intent: Build one consolidated tool layer for git, gh and Jira, and make the daemon's tool registry that layer. The workflow library calls it through the executor and no longer shells out. runGit, commitAndPushArtifacts, the github.ts wrappers and the existing git_* tools are all cut over in this one change, with no shims. Coverage is a curated, typed tool per operation family for git, gh and Jira. Jira gets its own agent-facing tools beside the GitHub ones, wrapping Atlassian's official acli so auth stays with the user's CLI session. Cross-cutting hooks, such as 'refresh tracker status after a pull or push', are executor-level post-execution hooks keyed by tool name. They run synchronously after the call, and a hook failure is non-fatal and is reported alongside the tool result. Each tool declares an output schema. The executor validates results, and a generic typed call helper infers the result type for the workflow library. Where a tool's CLI output is not already structured, the cheap model converts the tool response to the tool's declared output schema, and the executor's schema validation is the safety net: a response that does not validate is a tool failure and is never passed on. Deterministic parsing stays preferred where the CLI gives structured output (gh --json, git porcelain, acli JSON). Destructive operations (force push, reset --hard, clean, branch/release/issue deletion) send an approval request over IPC to whichever client is attached, each time. If no client answers within the timeout, the call is denied.
body.scopeBoundary: The scope covers the tool registry as the single layer for git, gh and Jira, the cutover of every workflow and daemon call site that shells out to them, the executor hook mechanism, output schemas with validation, and the per-call approval of destructive operations. It does not cover a separate in-process library beside the registry, a hook bus outside the executor, one tool per subcommand, direct Jira REST calls or stored Jira tokens, a phased migration with shims, any Jira CLI other than acli, a blanket allow-all for destructive operations, or auto-approval when no client is attached.
nonGoals: No separate typed in-process library alongside the registry; the registry is the only layer
No hook bus outside the executor; hooks are not registered in workflow code or per-wrapper
No one-tool-per-subcommand mirroring of git, gh or Jira
No direct Jira REST calls or stored Jira API tokens in the daemon
No phased or dual-path migration; no compatibility shims left for the old runGit/github.ts shell-outs
No support for Jira CLIs other than acli
No unguarded destructive operations; there is no blanket allow-all bypass for agents
No auto-approval of destructive calls when no client is attached; they are denied after the timeout
Typed service layer, with tools as thin adapters
Shared low-level exec helper only
Hooks declared inside each tool's own definition
Event bus: tools emit events, subscribers react
No hook mechanism now; only guarantee a single call path
Typed tools for common operations plus a raw passthrough tool per CLI/API
Generate tools from the CLI help text or OpenAPI spec
Direct Jira REST via undici with an API token or OAuth stored in daemon config
Jira via an MCP server the daemon connects to
Staged: wrappers become thin shims over the registry
New tools first, migrate call sites per story later
Synchronous, hook failure fails the tool call
Asynchronous fire-and-forget
Single supported CLI: community jira-cli (ankitpokhrel)
Adapter per CLI behind one tool surface
Tools return structured JSON by convention; workflow code casts or parses per call site
Tools return raw CLI text; workflow code parses it
Explicit opt-in flag per destructive call, enforced by the tool
Exclude destructive operations from the layer entirely
Separate destructive tools, hidden from agents by default and enabled via config
Approval prompt for agent callers only; workflow code declares its destructive ops up front and is pre-authorised by the approved plan
Destructive tools are refused outright unless the caller passes an explicit per-call confirmation token from the user

decisions.chosen: Tool registry is the layer; workflow calls it through the executor
ruledOut: Typed service layer, with tools as thin adapters
Shared low-level exec helper only
decisions.reason: The idea names runGit, commitAndPushArtifacts and github.ts in the workflow library on one side and the daemon's separate git_* tool registry on the other.

decisions.chosen: Executor-level post-execution hooks keyed by tool name
ruledOut: Hooks declared inside each tool's own definition
Event bus: tools emit events, subscribers react
No hook mechanism now; only guarantee a single call path
decisions.reason: Since the point of the layer is a single place for hooks like 'refresh tracker status after a pull or push', how should hooks attach to the tools?

decisions.chosen: Curated typed tool per operation family
ruledOut: Typed tools for common operations plus a raw passthrough tool per CLI/API
Generate tools from the CLI help text or OpenAPI spec
decisions.reason: The hook mechanism keys on tool name (decision 2), so every mutating operation must be a distinct named tool, not a subcommand argument inside a generic one.

decisions.chosen: Shell out to a local Jira CLI (e.g. jira-cli / acli)
ruledOut: Direct Jira REST via undici with an API token or OAuth stored in daemon config
Jira via an MCP server the daemon connects to
decisions.reason: How should the Jira tools authenticate, given the project principle that auth stays with the user's local CLI sessions and the daemon makes no direct cloud REST calls?

ruledOut: Staged: wrappers become thin shims over the registry
New tools first, migrate call sites per story later
decisions.reason: How should the existing workflow shell-outs (runGit, commitAndPushArtifacts, github.ts wrappers) and the current git_* tools move onto the consolidated layer?

decisions.chosen: Synchronous, hook failure is non-fatal and reported
ruledOut: Synchronous, hook failure fails the tool call
Asynchronous fire-and-forget
decisions.reason: Follows from decision 2 (executor-level post-execution hooks keyed by tool name) and 5 (workflow now depends on the executor for git/gh results, so hook behavior affects workflow correctness).

decisions.chosen: Single supported CLI: Atlassian's official acli
ruledOut: Single supported CLI: community jira-cli (ankitpokhrel)
Adapter per CLI behind one tool surface
decisions.reason: Which Jira CLI should the Jira tools wrap, given that the tools must behave deterministically and the daemon cannot support every CLI's differing command surface and output format?

decisions.chosen: Each tool declares an output schema; executor validates and a generic typed call helper infers the result type
ruledOut: Tools return structured JSON by convention; workflow code casts or parses per call site
Tools return raw CLI text; workflow code parses it
decisions.reason: The registry is the only layer and the workflow library must call it through the executor, but tools today return generic results while workflow code (e.g. commitAndPushArtifacts, github.ts wrappers) relies on typed return values.

decisions.chosen: Route destructive calls through an approval prompt to the user
ruledOut: Explicit opt-in flag per destructive call, enforced by the tool
Exclude destructive operations from the layer entirely
Separate destructive tools, hidden from agents by default and enabled via config
decisions.reason: Prior decisions made the registry the single layer shared by agents and workflows with full-operation coverage, so the existing git_* tools' safety posture must be settled explicitly.

decisions.chosen: Approval request via IPC to whichever client is attached; deny if none within timeout
ruledOut: Approval prompt for agent callers only; workflow code declares its destructive ops up front and is pre-authorised by the approved plan
Destructive tools are refused outright unless the caller passes an explicit per-call confirmation token from the user
decisions.reason: Follows from decision 9 (approval prompt for destructive calls) combined with decision 1 (workflows and agents share the same registry).
